sub: OOP concepts, applications and the OOP process
q: A Rectangle class has virtual setWidth(int) and setHeight(int). Square is derived publicly from Rectangle and overrides both so that setting either dimension sets the other as well, keeping the sides equal. Existing code that was written and tested against Rectangle — void grow(Rectangle& r) { r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(4); assert(r.area() == 20); } — now fails when a Square is passed to it. Which design principle does this hierarchy violate?

opts.A: Open/Closed Principle — grow() has to be modified every time a new subclass of Rectangle is introduced
opts.B: Interface Segregation Principle — Square is forced to depend on setter functions it has no use for
opts.C: Liskov Substitution Principle — Square cannot be used through a Rectangle reference without breaking the behaviour that Rectangle's existing clients were written against
opts.D: Single Responsibility Principle — Rectangle is made responsible both for storing its dimensions and for computing its area

exp: Substitutability is a behavioural contract, not merely a compilable one: Rectangle's clients rely on setWidth leaving the height alone, and Square breaks that guarantee, so a Square object is not a valid stand-in for a Rectangle. The Interface Segregation reading is the tempting one, but Square is not forced to depend on methods it does not use — it implements both setters, just with different behaviour; and grow() was never modified, so nothing here contradicts the Open/Closed Principle either.

sub: OOP concepts, applications and the OOP process
q: A PayrollReport class builds its own data source: its constructor executes db_ = new MySqlConnection(...). The team now wants to exercise PayrollReport against a test double, and later against a different database product, without editing PayrollReport at all. Which restructuring applies the Dependency Inversion Principle?

opts.A: Declare an abstract base class IDataSource with pure virtual query functions, make MySqlConnection derive from it, and pass an IDataSource& into PayrollReport's constructor
opts.B: Make MySqlConnection a singleton reached through a static instance() function, so that the database object is created in exactly one place
opts.C: Derive PayrollReport from MySqlConnection, so that the database operations become inherited member functions
opts.D: Keep the existing constructor but change db_ from private to protected, so that a test-only class derived from PayrollReport can replace it

exp: Dependency inversion means the high-level policy and the low-level detail both depend on an abstraction, and that the choice of concrete type is made outside the class that uses it — an abstract base plus constructor injection achieves exactly that. The singleton is the most tempting alternative because it does centralise construction, but PayrollReport still names MySqlConnection in its code, so no substitute can be supplied; deriving PayrollReport from MySqlConnection asserts a false is-a relationship and does not remove the concrete dependency either.

sub: OOP concepts, applications and the OOP process
q: A C++ class TimedCache must reuse the implementation of an existing class Buffer, must override Buffer's virtual function onFull(), and must not allow its own clients to call any of Buffer's public member functions on a TimedCache object. Which mechanism satisfies all three requirements at once?

opts.A: Hold a Buffer object as a private data member of TimedCache and forward to it
opts.B: Derive publicly from Buffer and then bring the unwanted inherited members into TimedCache's private section with using-declarations
opts.C: Declare TimedCache a friend of Buffer so it can reach Buffer's internals without inheriting from it
opts.D: Derive privately from Buffer

exp: Private inheritance expresses "is implemented in terms of": the derived class may override the base's virtual functions and use its protected members, while the base's public interface does not become part of the derived class's interface and outside code cannot convert a TimedCache to a Buffer. Composition is the correct default and is the tempting answer here, but an enclosing class cannot override the virtual functions of a member object; and public inheritance with private using-declarations still leaves the base subobject reachable through a Buffer reference or pointer.

sub: OOP concepts, applications and the OOP process
q: A department's system handles exactly three record types, which have not changed in a decade, but analysts add new operations over those records — a new levy calculation, a new export format — several times a year. The code today is procedural: one function per operation, branching internally on a record-type tag. A developer proposes converting it so that each record type becomes a class and every operation becomes a virtual function. Which assessment correctly states the trade-off?

opts.A: It is an improvement whatever the change profile, because an operation added to the base class automatically gives every record type a correct implementation of it
opts.B: It moves the cost of change to the wrong place: every new operation must now be added to each class in the hierarchy, whereas the procedural form confines a new operation to one new function — dynamic dispatch pays off when new types are frequent, not when new operations are
opts.C: It is an improvement because virtual dispatch eliminates the type tag and the branch on it, and that branch is the dominant cost in code of this kind
opts.D: The choice is neutral for future maintenance, because a table of virtual functions and a switch on a type tag are mechanically equivalent to each other

exp: The two decompositions differ in which axis of change is cheap: class hierarchies absorb new types without touching existing code but spread each new operation across every class, while a function branching on a tag absorbs new operations in one place but must be edited for every new type. Option D is the trap — the two forms are indeed inter-convertible in expressive power, which is exactly why the real difference is where future edits land rather than what can be expressed; and a base-class implementation inherited by every record type is a default, not a correct one.

sub: OOP concepts, applications and the OOP process
q: In a college system, a Course object refers to the Student objects enrolled in it. A student may be enrolled in several courses at once, exists before and after any particular course, and must continue to exist when a course object is destroyed at the end of a term. Which UML relationship describes this, and which C++ member is the faithful realisation of it?

opts.A: Composition (filled diamond); Course holds std::vector<Student>, storing the students by value
opts.B: Aggregation (hollow diamond); Course holds std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Student>>, since unique_ptr records that a student belongs to one course at a time
opts.C: Aggregation (hollow diamond); Course holds std::vector<Student*>, non-owning pointers to Student objects whose lifetime is managed elsewhere
opts.D: Composition (filled diamond); Course holds std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Student>>, so that the students are destroyed with the course

exp: Aggregation is the whole-part relationship in which the part is shareable and outlives the whole, and the standard C++ realisation is a non-owning handle to an object owned by some other part of the system. Option B is the tempting one because it names the right relationship, but unique_ptr asserts exclusive ownership and destroys the Student when the Course is destroyed — that is precisely composition's lifetime rule, and it also makes enrolment in a second course impossible.

sub: OOP concepts, applications and the OOP process
q: A module exposes void generate(const Report& r, bool asPdf); where the second argument selects between two entirely different formatting routines inside the function body, so the caller has to know how the callee is internally organised in order to pass the right value. In the standard coupling taxonomy, which form of coupling does that second parameter introduce?

opts.A: Data coupling
opts.B: Stamp coupling
opts.C: Common coupling
opts.D: Control coupling

exp: Control coupling is present when one module passes another an element of control — a flag, a mode, a switch value — that directs which path the callee takes, which is why it leaks the callee's internal structure to the caller and is normally removed by splitting the function or by dispatching on a polymorphic object instead. Data coupling would be the answer if the bool were consumed as ordinary data rather than as a selector; common coupling refers to modules sharing global data, and neither module here does.

sub: OOP concepts, applications and the OOP process

opts.A: It hands callers a modifiable handle to the internal container, so transactions can be added or removed without going through post(), and the class can no longer guarantee that balance_ agrees with txns_
opts.B: It returns a reference to a member, which dangles as soon as the Account object is copied
opts.C: The private specifier is defeated because member functions are permitted to read private data; txns_ should be declared protected so that only derived classes can reach it
opts.D: The only defect is one of efficiency — returning the vector by value would copy the entire history on each call, so returning a reference is right and the design is sound

exp: Encapsulation means the class controls every change to its own state, not merely that a member carries the private keyword; a non-const reference handed out by a public function exports write access to that state and destroys the invariant post() exists to maintain, and the usual repair is to return const std::vector<Txn>& or an iterator range. Option D correctly identifies that copying the vector would be expensive, which is what makes it tempting, but it draws the wrong conclusion — the reference being cheap does not make an unrestricted, non-const one safe.

sub: OOP concepts, applications and the OOP process
q: In structured development, analysis yields data flow diagrams and a data dictionary, which must then be transformed into a different kind of artefact — a structure chart of functional modules — before coding can begin. Object-oriented development is instead commonly described as "seamless". What does that description actually refer to?

opts.A: That object-oriented CASE tools generate the implementation directly from the analysis diagrams, so the design phase is no longer performed
opts.B: That the same abstractions — the classes and the relationships between them — are carried forward and progressively refined from analysis into design and into code, so no translation into a different kind of model is required at each phase boundary, which is what makes iterating back and forth between the phases cheap
opts.C: That requirements need not be recorded separately, because the class diagram produced during design serves as the requirements specification
opts.D: That testing merges into coding, because encapsulation confines every defect to the class containing it and so removes the need for integration testing

exp: The claim of seamlessness is about representational continuity: an object identified during analysis becomes a class refined during design and a class defined in code, so there is no notational gap of the kind that separates a data flow diagram from a structure chart, and revisiting an earlier phase therefore does not mean redoing a translation. Option D is the closest thing to a real benefit on the list — encapsulation does localise many defects — but it does not describe seamlessness, and objects that collaborate still have to be tested together.

sub: Classes, objects, member functions and memory allocation
q: A class has four non-static data members, one static data member and eight member functions. Ten objects of this class are created. Ignoring alignment padding, what is replicated inside each of the ten objects?

opts.A: All of the data members and all eight member functions, so that each object can dispatch its own calls without any lookup
opts.B: The four non-static data members and the static data member, but not the member functions
opts.C: Only the four non-static data members; the static data member exists once for the whole class and the member function code exists once and is shared
opts.D: The four non-static data members and the eight member functions, while the static data member exists once for the whole class

exp: Member function code is generated once per class and shared by every object, which receives the address of the object it is to work on; only the non-static data members are laid out inside an object, and a static data member has a single shared definition outside every object. Option D is the classic misconception — objects do not carry copies of their member functions, which is why adding a non-virtual member function to a class does not make its objects any bigger. Adding the first virtual function is the exception, since a vtable-based implementation then has to store a pointer inside each object.

sub: Classes, objects, member functions and memory allocation
q: The body of class Counter contains the line `static int instances;` and its constructor increments that member. Every translation unit compiles, but the link fails with an undefined reference to `Counter::instances`. What is missing?

opts.A: `instances` must be initialised in the member-initialiser list of every constructor of Counter
opts.B: `instances` must be declared `public`, because a linker symbol cannot be emitted for a private member
opts.C: `instances` must be declared `const`, because a static data member cannot otherwise be given storage
opts.D: A definition at namespace scope in exactly one source file, such as `int Counter::instances = 0;` — the line inside the class body is only a declaration (since C++17 the member may instead be declared `inline` in the class, which supplies the definition)

exp: A non-inline static data member declared in the class body is only declared there; it needs exactly one definition at namespace scope to acquire storage and a linker symbol, which is why the error appears at link time and not at compile time. A member-initialiser list cannot serve, because it initialises the object under construction, and a static member belongs to the class rather than to any object.

sub: Classes, objects, member functions and memory allocation
q: A class computes an expensive result the first time it is asked for and stores it in a data member so later requests are cheap. The accessor that does this must remain usable on objects of the class that are themselves declared `const`. Which is the correct way to let the accessor write to that member while remaining a `const` member function?

opts.A: Declare the cache data member `mutable`
opts.B: Cast the constness away inside the accessor with a `const_cast` on `this` and write through the result
opts.C: Declare the cache data member `static`, so that it is not covered by any object's constness
opts.D: Overload the accessor on constness and let the non-const overload perform the update

exp: `mutable` exempts a single data member from the constness the enclosing object imposes, so a `const` member function may still assign to it — this is the sanctioned way to implement a lazily filled cache. The `const_cast` route is the tempting alternative, but writing to an object that was itself declared `const` through such a cast is undefined behaviour; and the non-const overload in D would never be selected for a `const` object in the first place.

sub: Classes, objects, member functions and memory allocation
exp: `P a[3];` default-constructs three elements, so the shared counter reaches 3, and `P b = a[0];` copy-initialises a fourth object from an lvalue, where no copy can be elided, so the user-provided copy constructor increments the counter once more. Answering 3 is the trap: it counts the array and forgets that the copy constructor was written to increment `n` as well.

sub: Classes, objects, member functions and memory allocation

opts.A: It is illegal: `v` is private to each individual object, so reading another object's `v` requires M to declare itself a friend
opts.B: It is legal only because `bigger` is a `const` member function; a non-const member function could not read another object's `v`
opts.C: It is legal only because `o` is a reference; the same expression on a parameter of type M taken by value would not compile
opts.D: It is legal: access control is granted per class, not per object, so a member function of M may read the private members of any M object it can name

exp: Access specifiers apply to the class as a whole, not to individual objects, so any member function of M may touch the private members of every M it can reach; a class never needs a friend declaration to see into its own type, which is what makes comparison and copy operations writable at all. Constness of `bigger` and the reference-ness of `o` are irrelevant to access — a by-value M parameter would be readable in exactly the same way.

sub: Classes, objects, member functions and memory allocation

opts.A: edd
opts.B: ed
opts.C: de
opts.D: ded

exp: `q` is an automatic object, so its destructor runs when `main` returns — that is, after `'e'` has already been printed — while the object created on the free store is never passed to `delete`, so its destructor is simply never called. 'edd' is the tempting answer because it assumes the runtime destroys leaked free-store objects at program exit; it does not, and that is precisely why an unmatched `new` leaks resources rather than merely memory.

sub: Classes, objects, member functions and memory allocation
q: A Widget has a default constructor that logs each time it runs. Comparing `Widget a[5];` with `std::vector<Widget> v; v.reserve(5);`, how many times does the default constructor run in each case?

opts.A: Five times for the array and five times for the reserve, since both set aside room for five Widgets
opts.B: Five times for the array, and not at all for the reserve: reserve only acquires raw capacity, leaving the vector's size at 0 with no elements constructed
opts.C: Not at all for the array, since array elements are constructed lazily on first use, and five times for the reserve
opts.D: Once for the array, which then copies that element into the other four slots, and once for the reserve

exp: An array of class type default-initialises every one of its elements at the point of declaration, so all five Widgets exist immediately. reserve() is the opposite: it only guarantees capacity for five, allocating raw storage without constructing anything, so size() stays 0 until elements are actually inserted. Option C inverts the array case — there is no lazy construction of array elements — and resize(5), not reserve(5), is the vector call that would construct five objects.

sub: Classes, objects, member functions and memory allocation
q: `Widget* p = new Widget[10];` allocates ten objects, and the code later releases them with `delete p;`. What does the C++ standard say about this?

opts.A: The behaviour is undefined: storage obtained from a `new[]` expression must be released with `delete[]`, which is the form that destroys every element
opts.B: It is well defined — `delete` consults the element count recorded with the allocation and destroys all ten objects
opts.C: It is well defined — exactly one destructor runs and the remaining nine objects leak
opts.D: It is well defined when `Widget` has a trivial destructor and undefined only when the destructor is non-trivial

exp: The standard requires the form of the delete-expression to match the form of the new-expression that produced the pointer; mismatching them is undefined behaviour, and only `delete[]` is obliged to destroy each element and release the array allocation. Option C is the most tempting distractor because it describes what some implementations appear to do, but 'one destructor runs and the rest leak' is not a guarantee the language makes, and there is no exemption for trivial destructors either.

sub: Classes, objects, member functions and memory allocation
q: A class has no data members and no virtual functions. Why can `sizeof` applied to that class never yield 0?

opts.A: Because every object carries a hidden pointer to its class's run-time type information
opts.B: Because two distinct complete objects of the same type are required to have distinct addresses, which would be impossible if a complete object occupied no storage
opts.C: Because the compiler must store the addresses of the class's member functions inside each object
opts.D: Because alignment rules round every object up to at least the size of a machine word

exp: Distinct complete objects of the same type must be distinguishable by address — an array of them must have addressable elements — so a complete object always occupies at least one byte, and its exact size beyond that is up to the implementation. There is no run-time type information pointer to blame here since the class has no virtual functions, and member function addresses are never stored inside objects.

sub: Classes, objects, member functions and memory allocation
q: A class currently has no virtual functions. On a typical implementation that dispatches virtual calls through a per-class virtual table, which single change to the class would be expected to increase `sizeof` for its objects?

opts.A: Adding a static data member to the class
opts.B: Adding one more non-virtual member function
opts.C: Declaring the class's destructor `virtual`
opts.D: Adding a `friend` declaration for a free function

exp: Giving a class its first virtual function — and a virtual destructor counts as one — makes a vtable-based implementation embed a virtual-table pointer in every object, which is the usual reason a class's objects suddenly grow. A static data member lives once outside every object, an ordinary member function is shared code, and a friend declaration only grants access rights; none of those three adds per-object storage.

sub: Classes, objects, member functions and memory allocation
q: A header defines class C. One member function, `f`, is defined inside the class body; another, `g`, is only declared inside the body and then defined below the class in the same header as `void C::g() { ... }`. When several translation units include this header, the link fails with a multiple-definition error for `C::g` but not for `C::f`. Why?

opts.A: A function defined inside the class body is given internal linkage, so every translation unit gets its own private copy that cannot clash
opts.B: The in-body definition is only a declaration; the compiler regenerates the body at each call site, so no symbol for `C::f` ever exists
opts.C: A function defined inside the class body is always expanded at the call site, so the linker never sees a definition for it
opts.D: A function defined inside the class body is implicitly `inline`, and an inline function may be defined identically in every translation unit; `C::g` is not implicitly inline, so it must be marked `inline` or moved into a single source file

exp: Defining a member function inside the class body makes it implicitly `inline`, and the one-definition rule specifically permits an inline function to be defined once in each translation unit provided the definitions are identical; an out-of-class definition sitting in a header is an ordinary external definition and breaks that rule the moment two translation units include it. `inline` does not confer internal linkage — the definitions still denote one entity with one address — and it is not a promise that any call is expanded in place.

sub: Constructors and destructors

opts.B: It does not compile, because the mem-initialiser list must follow declaration order
opts.D: Either 12 or 21, because the order of member initialisation is unspecified

exp: Non-static data members are initialised in the order they are declared in the class, never in the order they happen to appear in the mem-initialiser list, so x(1) runs before y(2) and 1 is printed first. 21 is the trap of reading the list top to bottom; the mismatch draws a warning such as -Wreorder but the code is well-formed, and the order is fixed by the language rather than left to the implementation.

sub: Constructors and destructors

opts.D: Nothing, because calling a virtual function while the D sub-object is still unconstructed is undefined behaviour

exp: While a base class constructor is running, the object's dynamic type is that base class, so a virtual call made from B's constructor resolves to B::f even though the complete object will be a D. The behaviour is well defined, not undefined, and that is exactly what makes the pitfall dangerous: the derived override is silently skipped instead of the program failing loudly.

sub: Constructors and destructors
q: A class X declares a constructor with the signature X(X other), taking its parameter by value. How does the compiler treat that declaration?

opts.A: It is accepted, but every copy recurses without end and overflows the stack at run time
opts.B: It is accepted, and the compiler passes the argument by reference anyway because the copy is elided
opts.C: It is accepted, and behaves as a copy constructor for any class that owns no dynamically allocated memory
opts.D: It is rejected at compile time: a constructor for X whose only parameter is an X by value is ill-formed

exp: A constructor for X whose first parameter is X by value, with no other parameters or with all the rest defaulted, is ill-formed and must be diagnosed, because binding that by-value parameter would itself require invoking a copy constructor. The tempting answer is runtime infinite recursion; the recursion is real in principle, which is precisely why the language forbids the declaration rather than letting it compile and then loop.

sub: Constructors and destructors
q: A class owns a raw pointer and therefore declares a destructor to free it. It declares no other special member function. Which special members does the compiler still supply?

opts.A: The copy constructor and copy assignment operator are implicitly deleted, because a user-declared destructor suppresses them
opts.B: The copy constructor and copy assignment operator are still supplied, but no move constructor or move assignment is declared, so intended moves silently copy
opts.C: The move constructor and move assignment operator are still supplied, while the copy operations are implicitly deleted
opts.D: No copy or move operation is supplied at all once any special member function is user-declared

exp: A user-declared destructor blocks the implicit declaration of the move constructor and move assignment operator, while the copy operations continue to be implicitly declared (their implicit definition in this situation is deprecated, but they exist). So std::move on such an object still compiles and merely copies the raw pointer, producing the double free the destructor was written to prevent, which is the Rule of Five in one sentence. Option A inverts the rule: it is the moves, not the copies, that the destructor suppresses.

sub: Constructors and destructors
q: Given struct Buffer { Buffer(int n); }; and void consume(Buffer);, the call consume(64) currently compiles. What changes if the constructor is marked explicit?

opts.A: Buffer b(64); stops compiling, while consume(64) still converts implicitly as before
opts.B: Nothing changes for consume(64), because explicit constrains conversion operators rather than constructors
opts.C: consume(64) and Buffer b = 64; both stop compiling, while consume(Buffer(64)) still compiles
opts.D: Both consume(64) and consume(Buffer(64)) stop compiling, because explicit forbids passing a Buffer by value

exp: explicit removes a constructor from consideration for implicit conversions and for copy-initialisation, so an int can no longer turn itself into a Buffer at a call site or across an = sign, while direct-initialisation and an explicitly written Buffer(64) are untouched. explicit applies to constructors as well as to conversion functions, which is why option B is wrong.

sub: Constructors and destructors
q: A constructor is written as Widget(int n) : Widget(), count(n) {}, where Widget() is another constructor of the same class and count is a data member. The compiler rejects it. Why?

opts.A: Delegation is permitted only from the default constructor to a parameterised one, not in this direction
opts.B: count would be initialised twice, and initialising a member twice is forbidden
opts.C: A delegating constructor must be declared after the constructor it targets
opts.D: A mem-initialiser that names the constructor's own class must be the only entry in the list

exp: When a mem-initialiser designates the constructor's own class it is a delegation, and the language requires it to stand alone, because the target constructor completely constructs the object before the delegating constructor's body starts; anything else the delegating constructor wants must be done in that body, here as count = n;. Delegation has no required direction, and the order in which constructors are declared inside the class is irrelevant.

sub: Constructors and destructors
q: Base declares a virtual destructor and Derived inherits from it publicly. Code executes Base* p = new Derived[3]; and later delete[] p;. What is the outcome?

opts.A: Undefined behaviour, because for an array the operand's static element type must match the dynamic element type, and a virtual destructor does not rescue it
opts.B: Well defined and correct, because the virtual destructor ensures all three Derived destructors run
opts.C: Only the first element is destroyed correctly, and the other two are leaked
opts.D: It fails to compile, because a Base* cannot be initialised from an array of Derived

exp: Array deletion is undefined when the static type of the operand differs from the dynamic type of the array elements: delete[] walks the array using sizeof(Base) while the elements are spaced by sizeof(Derived), so the addresses it destroys are not the objects. A virtual destructor fixes only the single-object case and cannot correct the element stride, which is why option B is the trap and why arrays of derived objects should never be held through a base pointer. The initialisation itself does compile, since Derived* converts to Base*.

sub: Constructors and destructors
q: In C++11 and later, an exception escapes the destructor of a class that has no bases or members with throwing destructors, and whose destructor carries no exception specification of its own. What happens?

opts.A: It propagates like an exception from any other function and can be caught by an enclosing handler
opts.B: The program is ill-formed and the compiler rejects the destructor
opts.C: std::terminate is called, because a destructor is implicitly noexcept unless declared otherwise
opts.D: It propagates unless the destructor is running during stack unwinding, in which case it is silently swallowed

exp: Since C++11 a destructor with no exception specification of its own is implicitly noexcept unless one of its base or member destructors is itself potentially throwing — which the stem rules out — so an escaping exception here crosses a noexcept boundary and std::terminate runs without any enclosing handler being consulted. Option A is the pre-C++11 answer; declaring the destructor noexcept(false) restores it, but even then an exception thrown while another is already unwinding the stack terminates the program, which is the underlying reason destructors should not throw.

sub: Constructors and destructors
q: A struct with two public int members was routinely created with Point p;. After a constructor Point(int x, int y) is added to it, every such line stops compiling. What explains this?

opts.A: The struct is no longer an aggregate, and a non-aggregate cannot be default-initialised
opts.B: Declaring any constructor stops the compiler from implicitly declaring a default constructor
opts.C: A class with a user-declared constructor can only be created with new
opts.D: The implicit default constructor is still declared, but is now implicitly deleted because the int members have no initialisers

exp: The default constructor is implicitly declared only when the class has no user-declared constructor of any kind, so adding Point(int, int) removes it and Point p; then finds no viable constructor; writing Point() = default; alongside brings it back. Option D is the near-miss: nothing deletes the default constructor here, it is simply never declared, and members of built-in type leave a default constructor uninitialised rather than deleted.

sub: Polymorphism, function and operator overloading
q: Which of the following operators can be overloaded in C++?

opts.A: The scope resolution operator ::
opts.B: The member selection operator . applied to an object
opts.C: The class member access operator ->
opts.D: sizeof

exp: operator-> can be overloaded, and doing so is what makes smart-pointer and proxy classes usable with pointer syntax; the compiler applies the overload repeatedly until a real pointer is produced. The other three are on the short fixed list the language declines to make overloadable — ::, ., .*, ?:, sizeof, typeid and alignof — a list to be learned rather than derived, since the members do not share one reason: :: and . take a name on the right, while sizeof, typeid and alignof are resolved against a type. Option B is the tempting one: -> is overloadable while the closely related . is not, and the asymmetry is deliberate rather than an oversight.

sub: Polymorphism, function and operator overloading
q: Base declares both void print() and void print(int). Derived, which inherits publicly from Base, declares only void print(int). What happens at the call d.print(), where d is a Derived object?

opts.A: It compiles and calls Base::print(), because public inheritance makes all of Base's members available
opts.B: It fails to compile, because Derived::print hides every Base overload of that name regardless of signature
opts.C: It compiles and calls Derived::print(int) with a default-constructed int argument
opts.D: It compiles only if Base::print() is declared virtual

exp: Name lookup stops at the first scope in which the name appears, so finding print in Derived means Base's scope is never searched — overload resolution then runs on the single candidate print(int) and fails for a call with no arguments. The hiding is by name, not by signature, which is why option A's reasoning breaks down even though the member genuinely is inherited and accessible; writing using Base::print; inside Derived pulls the base overloads back into the same scope and makes the call work. Declaring the base function virtual, as option D suggests, changes which override runs but has no effect on name lookup.

sub: Polymorphism, function and operator overloading
q: A Money class overloads multiplication as a member function, Money operator*(int n) const. The expression m * 2 compiles, but 2 * m does not. What is the reason?

opts.A: The int operand must be converted with an explicit cast before any overloaded operator will accept it
opts.B: Member operator functions can only be used when both operands are of the same class type
opts.C: The overload must be declared with the commutative keyword for either operand order to work
opts.D: A member operator function is called on its left operand, so the left operand has to be a Money object; 2 * m would require int to have such a member

exp: For a binary member operator, the left operand is the implicit *this, so m * 2 rewrites to m.operator*(2) while 2 * m would need 2.operator*(m) — and a built-in type has no member functions. The fix is a non-member overload, Money operator*(int n, const Money& m), which receives both operands as ordinary parameters and so places no requirement on which side the class appears; this is the usual reason arithmetic operators are written as non-members. Option B is wrong in an instructive way: m * 2 is itself a member call with operands of different types, which is exactly what disproves it. C invents a keyword that does not exist.

sub: Polymorphism, function and operator overloading
q: A Counter class overloads both forms of ++. The conventional prefix form returns Counter& while the conventional postfix form returns Counter by value. What makes the postfix form unable to return a reference the way the prefix form does?

opts.A: Postfix must yield the value the object had before the increment, and that earlier value survives only as a local copy inside the operator, so returning a reference to it would leave a dangling reference
opts.B: Returning a reference from any operator that takes a dummy parameter is forbidden by the language
opts.C: Postfix increment is resolved at compile time, and compile-time binding cannot produce references
opts.D: The object is const during a postfix increment, so only a copy can be returned

exp: Prefix ++ leaves the incremented object itself as its result, so it can hand back *this, which outlives the call; postfix has to produce the old value, which the operator must save in a local before modifying the object, and that local is destroyed when the function returns. This is also why postfix is the more expensive of the two for a non-trivial class and why the prefix form is preferred in loops. Option D inverts the situation: the object is being modified, so it is emphatically not const — the copy is needed because of the value the caller expects, not because of constness.

sub: Polymorphism, function and operator overloading
q: Given only the overloads void f(int) and void f(double), which describes the calls f('a') and f(7L)?

opts.A: f('a') calls f(int); f(7L) is ambiguous and fails to compile
opts.B: Both calls select f(int), since integral types always prefer an integral parameter
opts.C: f('a') is ambiguous; f(7L) calls f(int)
opts.D: Both calls are ambiguous, because neither char nor long matches a parameter exactly

exp: char to int is an integral promotion, which overload resolution ranks strictly better than the char-to-double conversion, so f('a') has a unique best match; long to int and long to double are both ordinary conversions of the same rank, so neither candidate is better and f(7L) is ambiguous. Option B states the appealing but false rule that an integral argument always prefers an integral parameter — long is integral, yet it does not select f(int). The distinction that actually decides both calls is promotion versus conversion, not integral versus floating.

sub: Polymorphism, function and operator overloading
q: Two functions in the same scope are declared as int compute(int x) and double compute(int x). What is the result?

opts.A: They form a valid overload set; the compiler picks one from the type expected at the call site
opts.B: They form a valid overload set, but only if the calls always assign the result to a variable
opts.C: It is ill-formed: functions whose parameter lists are identical cannot be distinguished by return type alone
opts.D: It is valid, and the second declaration silently replaces the first

exp: Overload resolution examines only the arguments at the call site, so two candidates with identical parameter lists give it nothing to choose between and the second declaration is rejected where it stands, before any call is written. The reasoning behind options A and B is what makes them tempting — a call really can appear in a context that wants a particular type — but a context is not an argument, and an expression such as compute(1); in a discarded-value statement would have no expected type at all. Note that overloads may certainly differ in return type as long as their parameters also differ; it is sameness of parameters that is fatal.
